questions.question: Why does LinkedList implement the Deque interface?
options: To work as a queue (Queue) and a stack (Stack)
To have fast access by index
explanations: Correct. Deque (Double Ended Queue) allows using LinkedList as a queue and a stack, adding methods like offer(), poll(), push(), pop().
No. Fast index access is better in ArrayList.
No. LinkedList does not automatically sort elements.
No. LinkedList allows duplicates; it is not for unique elements.

questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of LinkedList?
explanations: Correct. LinkedList has O(n) random access because it must traverse the list from one end to the desired position.
No. LinkedList supports generics just like ArrayList.

questions.question: What is a node in a LinkedList?
options: An element with a reference to the previous and next one
An element with a numeric index
An element with a hash value
An element with a memory pointer
explanations: Correct. Each node contains the data and two references: one to the previous node and another to the next node.
No. It does not use numeric indexes; it uses references to nodes.
No. It does not use hashes; it uses direct references to other nodes.
No. Although it uses references, they are not direct memory pointers but references to objects.

questions.question: When is it preferable to use LinkedList over ArrayList?
options: When there are many insertions/removals and few lookups
When fast access by index is needed
When many elements need to be stored
When an alphabetical order is needed
explanations: Correct. LinkedList is better when the main operations are insertions and removals at the ends.
No. For fast access by index, ArrayList is better.
No. Both can store many elements, but ArrayList is more memory efficient.
No. Neither of them sorts automatically.
